arxiv-2109-12860.title: Classifying Dyads for Militarized Conflict Analysis
arxiv-2109-12860.creator: Niklas Stoehr Lucas Torroba Hennigen Samin Ahbab, Robert West Ryan Cotterell
arxiv-2109-12860.description: Abstract Understanding the origins of militarized conflict is a complex, yet important undertaking. Existing research seeks to build this understanding by considering bi-lateral relationships between entity pairs (dyadic causes) and multi-lateral relationships among multiple entities (systemic causes). The aim of this work is to compare these two causes in terms of how they correlate with conflict between two entities.

arxiv-2304-07151.title: End-to-End Learning with Multiple Modalities for System-Optimised Renewables Nowcasting
arxiv-2304-07151.creator: Rushil Vohra, Ali Rajaei , and Jochen L. Cremer
arxiv-2304-07151.description: Abstract With the increasing penetration of renewable power sources such as wind and solar, accurate short-term, nowcasting renewable power prediction is becoming increasingly important. This paper investigates the multi-modal (MM) learning and end-to-end (E2E) learning for nowcasting renewable power as an intermediate to energy management systems.

arxiv-2305-13388.title: The neural dynamics of auditory word recognition and integration
arxiv-2305-13388.creator: Jon Gauthier, Roger Levy
arxiv-2305-13388.description: A 2023 arXiv research paper by Jon Gauthier, Roger Levy. Listeners recognize and integrate words in rapid and noisy everyday speech by combining expectations about upcoming content with incremental sensory evidence. We present a computational model of word recognition which formalizes this perceptual process in Bayesian decision theory. We fit this model to explain scalp EEG signals recorded as subjects passively listened to a fictional story, revealing both the dynamics of the online auditory word recognition process and the neural correlates of the recognition and integration of words.

pmc-13246389.description: A peer-reviewed research article from Europe PMC (2026). RNA-protein (RNP) complexes regulate nearly every stage of gene expression and play central roles in viral infection and human disease. Despite decades of research, relatively few small molecules (SMs) have been shown to modulate RNP assemblies with mechanistic understanding. A major challenge in targeting RNA arises from the absence of well-defined SM binding pockets analogous to the catalytic active sites that guide conventional protein-directed drug discovery.
